Joe Pesci's Tommy DeVito walks into a room expecting to become a made man in Goodfellas. What happens next takes only a few seconds, but it's a moment audiences will never forget. That's the power of a great crime movie plot twist. Sometimes everything changes in an instant. Other times, the truth has been staring us in the face for the entire movie, and we only realize it when it's too late.

The Godfather Part II delivers a different kind of gut punch. Michael Corleone spends much of the movie trying to uncover who betrayed him, only to find the answer painfully close to home. That suspicion runs through many of the best gangster movies to watch after Goodfellas, where promises of loyalty rarely survive the first serious test.

Then there are movies that turn the audience into the sucker. In Primal Fear, Richard Gere's lawyer is certain he finally understands his client. The Usual Suspects plays an even longer con, letting a police interrogation shape almost everything we think we know until the final minutes.

Verbal's account gradually points toward another member of the gang as the elusive Söze.

Only after Verbal leaves the police station does Kujan recognize that names and details from his story came from objects scattered around the interrogation room. Goodfellas (1990)

7
The Outfit (2022)

Graham Moore's The Outfit is a wonderfully deceptive crime thriller starring Mark Rylance as Leonard Burling, a mild-mannered English tailor working in 1950s Chicago. When a dispute between rival criminal organizations erupts inside his shop, Leonard appears hopelessly outmatched by the violent gangsters surrounding him. His only apparent advantage is his ability to remain calm under extraordinary pressure.

The ending reveals that Leonard has been manipulating the criminals all along, planting forged messages supposedly from the powerful Chicago Outfit and exploiting their suspicions to turn them against one another. Even more surprisingly, the seemingly harmless tailor was once a ruthless criminal enforcer himself. Rylance's understated performance makes the revelation especially satisfying, as the man everyone dismissed turns out to have understood the situation better than anyone.

6
Reservoir Dogs (1992)

Quentin Tarantino's Reservoir Dogs begins in the aftermath of a botched diamond robbery, with the surviving criminals desperately trying to identify the police informant responsible. Suspicion rapidly spreads among the gang, particularly as the badly wounded Mr. Orange (Tim Roth) lies bleeding on the warehouse floor. Mr. White (Harvey Keitel) becomes increasingly protective of him, convinced that his younger associate deserves his loyalty.

Then Tarantino reveals that Mr. Orange is actually undercover police officer Freddy Newandyke. The revelation arrives well before the film's climax, allowing audiences to watch Mr. White defend the very person who betrayed him. When Orange finally confesses his identity, their relationship collapses in an instant. The devastating ending of Reservoir Dogs works because Tarantino makes the audience understand both men's perspectives, turning an elaborate criminal deception into something unexpectedly tragic.

Yet the movie's greatest achievement may be Noodles' refusal to give Max the revenge or absolution he seeks.

The Godfather Part II (1974)

Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather Part II contains one of cinema's most heartbreaking betrayals. Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) survives an assassination attempt at his Nevada compound and begins investigating which member of his organization helped his enemies. His suspicions eventually lead him to Havana, where his older brother Fredo (John Cazale) inadvertently reveals that he knows Johnny Ola, an associate of rival gangster Hyman Roth.

Fredo previously denied knowing Ola, making his careless remark an unmistakable admission of secret contact. Michael's realization that his own brother betrayed him leads to their devastating confrontation and, eventually, Fredo's murder on Michael's orders. The exact extent of Fredo's involvement remains uncertain, but his resentment toward Michael becomes painfully clear. Few crime movie twists carry such enormous emotional consequences, particularly because the betrayal exposes how completely Michael's pursuit of power has destroyed his family.

3
Primal Fear (1996)

Edward Norton delivered one of the most astonishing film debuts of the 1990s in Primal Fear. He plays Aaron Stampler, a frightened altar boy accused of murdering a prominent Chicago archbishop. Defense attorney Martin Vail (Richard Gere) believes his client is innocent, eventually discovering that Aaron apparently has a violent alternate personality named Roy, who emerges during periods Aaron cannot remember.

After Vail successfully secures a favorable outcome that sends Aaron for psychiatric treatment, his client accidentally reveals that he remembers something his supposed alternate personality did in court. Confronted by his lawyer, he drops the stutter and admits that the entire psychological defense was an act. There never was an innocent Aaron. Norton's transformation is extraordinary, but the devastating final revelation in Primal Fear makes Richard Gere's reaction equally memorable. Vail wins his case and discovers he's helped a calculating murderer escape responsibility.
